blocks.text: Letters of commendation belonged to ancient networks, so Paul’s question is not simply a rejection of references or accountability. Calling the Corinthians a letter “known and read by all” makes their shared life a public testimony, but the image should not turn people’s changed lives into a leader’s private credentials or marketing property.

Paul joins his confidence in this relationship to a denial of self-sufficiency: competence for this ministry comes from God, not from the workers themselves. The passage therefore holds together a visible relationship with the Corinthians and an account of ministry that does not make its leaders immune from review.

“The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” belongs to Paul’s contrast between kinds of covenant ministry in this chapter. It should not be reduced to a rejection of written Scripture, law, careful thinking, or evidence. Likewise, the chapter’s language about Moses’ veil, hardening, and the removal of the veil has received sharply differing Jewish and Christian interpretations; it cannot justify hostility toward Jews or portray living Judaism as a dead religion.

Verses 16–18 contain important uncertainties. Interpreters dispute both who is said to turn to the Lord in verse 16 and how “the Lord is the Spirit” in verse 17 should be understood. In verse 18, the underlying term may mean either beholding glory as in a mirror or reflecting glory. What remains clear in the passage is its description of Spirit-enabled transformation, while the precise visual image should be held with care.

The wider text of 2 Corinthians is preserved in substantial early manuscript witnesses: P46 contains most of the letter, P99 preserves portions, and major codices provide further witnesses with distinct textual profiles.
